sourceInformation.source: Jungle Hunt (1983 home release; 1982 Taito arcade original)
sourceInformation.tech: Three.js r180 (0.180.0), WebGPURenderer with WebGPU and WebGL 2 fallback; Rapier 3D 0.19.3; Gamepad API; Web Audio; WebRTC; AI Hub Session Protocol v1, client 1.4.0; esbuild 0.28.2
sourceInformation.artDirection: Stylized cel shading, ink outlines, warm printed-paper UI and layered geometric jungle scenery
sourceInformation.animation: Three.js AnimationMixer, AnimationClip and keyframe tracks; original run, swim, jump, hang, duck, cheer, vine swing and crocodile jaw animations
sourceInformation.audio: Original code-generated adventure music, percussion, effects and Animalese-style oscillator gibberish; music defaults to 10%; no audio files
sourceInformation.online: 1–4 player AI Hub ghost expeditions; standalone two-player direct WebRTC ghost races with manual invitation and answer
sourceInformation.testing: Headless Chromium 153, software WebGPU with GPU pixel readback and WebGL 2 fallback; full scripted expeditions with normal lives and attract-mode cheats; standard gamepad stub; emulated touch; Web Audio analyser; real two-page WebRTC; official AI Hub 2/4-seat and host-leave harness with 150 ms latency, 50 ms jitter and 5% loss. Physical controller and real phones: unknown. Multiplayer harness and touch checks also exercise the WebGL fallback; a two-page race mixes GPU and fallback rendering.
sourceInformation.research: Atari instruction manual, AtariAge screenshots, retro sound comparison and AI Hub protocol documentation

testingFeedback: Nine implementation or test-environment issues were caught and fixed: vine launch balance, boulder restitution and spacing, buffered checkpoint jumps, immediate menu focus, controller disconnect state, timer formatting, software WebGPU launch flags, stalled multi-page GPU initialization, and gameplay toasts overlapping menus.

Three blockers during development: the initial vine launch balance, headless WebGPU device loss, and stalled second-page GPU initialization. Launch flags, resource cleanup and a timed WebGL fallback resolved them.

The complete expedition with ordinary lives exposed balance problems hidden by the invincible attract demo. GPU pixel readback plus a minimal native WebGPU control isolated the browser configuration problem.
Early WebGPU screenshots: their blank canvases did not distinguish renderer device loss from headless capture behavior.
engineFeedback: Three.js AnimationMixer and TSL supported original character animation and one cel-shading system across WebGPU and WebGL 2.
Rapier restitution is combined with the floor by default, which damped boulders more than intended. Software WebGPU also needed additional Vulkan browser flags.
The four traversal modes, forgiving vine catches, controller menu focus and ghost-race lifecycle.
Verifying actual WebGPU output while keeping physics, animation and menu input testable without a display.
none; engine sources are unmodified. The application requests core WebGPU features and explicitly sets Rapier restitution mixing.
A native ink-outline material with consistent WebGPU and WebGL behavior would simplify this art direction.
promptFeedback: The four-act source, controller-first UX and explicit testing requirements gave the game a clear shape.
1983 identifies a home release; the original arcade game dates to 1982. Standalone multiplayer transport was unspecified.

aiHub.name: Jungle Zip
aiHub.description: Swing through the canopy, swim past snapping crocs and dodge a boulder stampede to rescue Professor Pip before teatime. A complete four-act ink-and-cel arcade adventure, solo or against ghost explorers.
aiHub.controls: WASD/arrows or left stick: move/swim; Space/Cross/A: jump/release; F/click/Square/X: swat/hold to rescue; S/Down/Circle/B: duck; Esc/Options: pause. Touch: left thumb moves, right tap jumps; hold to rescue.
